title: Authority Over Disease, Storm, and Demons
summary: Coming down from the mountain, Jesus heals a leper with a touch, heals a Roman centurion's servant with a word from a distance, and raises Peter's mother-in-law from a fever. Two would-be followers learn what following him costs. He calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee and frees two demon-possessed men on the far shore, whose town then asks him to leave.
story: Matthew has just finished the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5 to 7), which ended with the crowds astonished that Jesus taught as one who had authority. Chapters 8 and 9 now show that authority in action. The words of the mountain become deeds in the towns and on the lake. Matthew groups ten miracles across these two chapters, and the order is telling: the first people helped are a leper, a Gentile soldier, and a woman, all on the edges of respectable religious life. The chapter also begins a thread that runs to the end of the Gospel, the question of who will receive the kingdom. A pagan officer shows greater faith than Jesus has found in Israel, while a Gentile town, faced with a man restored and a herd lost, would rather Jesus went away.
historical:
These events take place in Galilee, the northern region of the land of Israel, which in Jesus' adult life was ruled by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. Antipas governed Galilee and Perea as tetrarch (a subordinate ruler under Rome) from 4 BC to AD 39. Capernaum, where Jesus made his base, was a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, near the border of Antipas's territory. Excavators there have uncovered a first-century house that was venerated by early Christians and later covered by an octagonal church in the fifth century; it is traditionally identified as Peter's house, though the identification cannot be proved.

The centurion is an officer who commanded about a hundred soldiers. Since Galilee was not under direct Roman administration at this time, many historians think he served in Antipas's forces, which were organized on the Roman pattern, rather than in a Roman legion; either way he was a Gentile. Luke tells the same story (Luke 7:1-10) and adds that Jewish elders spoke for him because he had built their synagogue. The far shore of the lake, the region of the Gadarenes, lay in the Decapolis, a league of Greek-speaking cities east of the Jordan. Mark and Luke call the place the region of the Gerasenes, and ancient manuscripts vary on the name; both Gadara and Gerasa were Decapolis cities, and the difference probably reflects which city's territory the storyteller named.
cultural:
Leprosy in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases, not only what is now called Hansen's disease. Under Leviticus 13 and 14, a person with such a disease was ritually unclean, had to live apart, and could return to community life only after a priest inspected him and the prescribed offerings were made. To touch a leper was to share his uncleanness. Jesus reverses the flow: his touch does not make him unclean, it makes the leper clean. He then sends the man to the priest, honoring the law of Moses and giving the priests evidence of what had happened.

A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile's house, and the centurion seems to know it, which may be part of why he asks only for a word. Burying a father was among the weightiest duties in Jewish life, one that took precedence over many other obligations, so Jesus' reply in verse 22 would have sounded shocking. Pigs, forbidden as food under Leviticus 11, mark the Gadarene region as Gentile country, and the tombs where the two men lived were places of uncleanness and, in popular belief, haunts of spirits.
literary: Matthew arranges chapters 8 and 9 in three groups of miracles separated by short scenes about discipleship. The first group (8:1-17) ends with a fulfillment quotation from Isaiah 53:4: “He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases.” Then comes a scene about the cost of following (8:18-22), and the second group begins with the storm and the demoniacs. Matthew tells these stories more briefly than Mark and Luke, trimming detail to keep attention on Jesus' authority and on faith. The storm story is framed by following: the disciples “followed Him” into the boat (8:23) right after Jesus has warned about what following means, so the boat becomes a picture of discipleship under pressure. Matthew also has two demoniacs where Mark 5 and Luke 8 have one, a pattern he repeats with two blind men in 20:30.

outline.t: A leper is cleansed by a touch
The centurion's faith and the servant healed from a distance
Peter's mother-in-law and many others healed
Two demon-possessed men freed in Gadarene country

doctrines.note: The chapter answers the question the disciples ask in verse 27: “What kind of man is this?” He heals by touch and by word, commands wind and sea as only God does in the Old Testament, and is recognized by demons as the Son of God. Matthew presents him as the promised Servant who carries our diseases.

Jesus' healings are signs that God's reign has arrived and is pushing back sickness, chaos, and evil powers. The centurion story extends the kingdom's banquet to people from east and west, while warning that those who assume a place at the table may lose it.

Faith here is trust in Jesus' power and willingness, seen most clearly in a Gentile who believes a word from Jesus is enough. The disciples' fear in the storm is called little faith, not no faith: they turn to him, but they do not yet grasp who is in the boat.

words.note: Katharizo, to cleanse or make clean. It is the word for ritual purification as well as healing, and in verses 2 and 3 it carries both: the leper is healed of disease and restored to the worshiping community. The leper's request is not only to be cured but to be made clean, and Jesus answers in the same word.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. The centurion understands authority from military life: orders given are carried out. He recognizes the same kind of authority in Jesus over sickness. The word links this chapter to 7:29, where Jesus taught with authority, and to 9:6, where he claims authority to forgive sins.

Oligopistos, of little faith. The word is nearly unique to Matthew and Luke in the New Testament, and Matthew uses it for the disciples several times (6:30, 8:26, 14:31, 16:8). It describes believers whose trust is real but too small for the situation, which is a gentler and more hopeful diagnosis than unbelief.

Hekatontarchos, centurion, literally a commander of a hundred. The title identifies the man as a professional soldier and almost certainly a Gentile. That such a man becomes Matthew's first example of great faith is one of the chapter's surprises.

christ: Matthew shows Jesus doing what the Old Testament says only God does. The Lord of Psalm 107 stills the storm and hushes the waves of the sea; here Jesus rebukes the winds and the sea, and the disciples ask what kind of man this is. Matthew also reads the healings through Isaiah 53, the song of the suffering Servant, which in its original setting speaks of one who bears the griefs and sins of others. By quoting it over a day of healings, Matthew hints that the Servant's work of carrying human burdens has already begun, and the reader who continues to the cross will see where that carrying leads. Jesus' self-description as the homeless Son of Man in verse 20 draws on Daniel 7, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom, yet here the one who will receive all authority has nowhere to lay his head.

hard.q: Why did Jesus let the demons destroy a whole herd of pigs, and why do the Gospels differ on the number of men?
hard.a:
The loss of the herd troubles modern readers, and it troubled the townspeople, who cared more about their livelihood than about two men set free. Interpreters offer several responses. Some note that Jesus permits rather than commands the destruction, and that the demons, not Jesus, drive the pigs into the sea, which shows their destructive intent toward everything they inhabit. Others see a visible demonstration, for the men and the town, that the spirits had really left. Others point out that the story's own emphasis falls on the value of two human beings compared with a herd of animals, a comparison Jesus makes explicitly elsewhere (12:12). None of these fully removes the sense of loss, and the text does not try to.

On the numbers, Mark 5 and Luke 8 tell of one man, the one who spoke, while Matthew mentions two. Many interpreters think Mark and Luke focus on the more prominent of the two, and Matthew, who also doubles the blind men in 20:30, may be concerned with the law's standard of two witnesses. Others take it as ordinary variation in how independent tellings handle detail. The place name also varies among the Gospels and the manuscripts, as noted above.

questions: The leper says “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” Which do you find harder to believe about God, that he is able or that he is willing?
A Gentile soldier is praised for faith while religious insiders are warned. Who might be the unexpected person of faith in your world?
The town asked Jesus to leave after he healed two men and cost them a herd. What losses make people wish Jesus would keep his distance?
